title: The Grassfed Scam: What Your Beef Label Isn’t Telling You
summary: Video from a beef and tallow brand arguing grass-fed, organic and pasture-raised labels are loosely defined greenwashing, and urging buyers to source from local or regenerative farms instead.

assertions.quote: But in 2016, the USDA dropped its official grass-fed definition. Now the label is self-p policed.

verdicts.note: USDA withdrew its grass-fed marketing standard in 2016; FSIS approves label claims case by case on producer documentation.

assertions.quote: Organic means that animals are not allowed any antibiotics or growth hormones.

verdicts.note: 7 CFR 205.238(c) says no animal treated with antibiotics, nor its products, may be sold as organic, and it bars hormones for growth, production or reproduction (205.237(b) also bars growth hormones and antibiotic-laced feed); sick animals must still be treated and then lose organic status.
ERS states organic livestock may only receive organic healthcare practices, which do not allow antibiotics or growth hormones.

assertions.quote: Cows must graze on pasture for at least 120 days per year

verdicts.note: EU organic standards require livestock outdoors part of the year and ruminants to get at least 60% of intake from forage, with fresh forage from grazing when conditions allow; describes EU, not US, rules.
7 CFR 205.237(c) requires ruminants to graze through the whole grazing season, at least 120 days a year, and to get on average at least 30 percent of their dry matter intake from pasture.

Since the 2010 clarification, organic cows must graze at least 120 days a year and get at least 30 percent of their nutrition from grazing; nonorganic cows have no pasture requirement (ERS describes the dairy rule specifically).

assertions.quote: organic does not mean grass-fed, grass-finished. They can still be fed a grain-fed diet and get the organic label.

verdicts.note: Organic rules require only seasonal pasture intake; the rest of the diet can be organic grain.

Under EU rules organic ruminant diets can include 0-40% concentrate feed, and some organic herds graze less than extensive non-organic ones, so organic does not mean fully grass-fed; grain feeding is limited, not banned.

7 CFR 205.239(d) calls organic ruminant slaughter stock 'typically grain finished' and allows feedlot finishing for up to one-fifth of the animal's life or 120 days, exempt from the 30 percent grazing rule; up to 70 percent of a ruminant's dry matter may be fed even during the grazing season (205.237(c)), provided the feed is organic.

assertions.quote: organic meat and dairy often come from industrialcale operations rather than small family farms.
free range only means that chickens were given access to the outdoors for some period of time each day.

verdicts.note: USDA free-range requires only some outdoor access and cage-free only no cages, with no space, duration or outdoor-quality minimums.

assertions.quote: For pasture rays, there is no legally binding USDA definition. The term is entirely unregulated.

verdicts.note: USDA has no codified pasture-raised standard; meaning depends on producer claims unless a third-party certification backs it.

assertions.quote: Byproducts like corn silage and distiller grains can change the fat and omega ratios in the meat compared to true pasture grazing.

verdicts.note: Grass-fed beef has more omega-3 and CLA and a better omega ratio, but the absolute amounts are small for health.

Cited controlled experiment: switching beef from grain to grass finishing raised intramuscular PUFA 45%, n-3 PUFA over 3-fold, EPA over 5-fold and DHA 129%, with no change in n-6; forage diets also lower SFA in meat.
Clark and Tilman cite Daley et al. (2010) that grass-fed beef has higher micronutrients and a fatty acid profile that might improve health outcomes; a secondary citation, not their own data.

assertions.quote: regenerative organic certified, American grass-fed association, and certified grass-fed by a greener world. These labels do a much better job

verdicts.note: ROC requires USDA Organic as a baseline and adds soil-health, animal-welfare and farmworker-fairness requirements.

assertions.quote: Grass-fed, organic, and pasture-raised all sound good, but unless you know who is verifying these claims, at the end of the day, it's just marketing.

verdicts.note: ERS describes the premium as resting on certified production differences that carry real costs at every supply-chain stage (certification, segregation, organic feed, transition), not on labelling alone, though willingness to pay also feeds the premium.
